en: The Legend of the Elder Madhudāyaka Pilindavaccha Chapter, Number 4 I gave a handful of honey to the Buddha, the Great Sage, who was seated upon the bank of the river Nerañjarā. Because of that deed, I have attained the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-phala*). May I never again fall into the states of woe. Through this root of merit, may I attain the supreme state of Buddhahood. May I be free from all defilements and become a Buddha, a teacher of gods and men. May I be endowed with the ten powers and the four grounds of self-confidence. May I be possessed of the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha. May I be adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great man. May I be surrounded by a retinue of a hundred thousand monks. May I be honored by the world with its gods, Māras, and Brahmās. May I be venerated by the assembly of ascetics, including gods and humans. May I be the refuge for the world. May I be the protector of the world. May I be the island for the world. May I be the light for the world. May I be the guide for the world. May I be the leader for the world. May I be the one who brings peace to the world. “On the bank of the river Sindhū,
my hermitage was well-prepared;
there I used to teach my pupils.”
This history along with its characteristics—
those who desire the Dhamma and are disciplined wish to hear this excellent teaching.
Having reached perfection in the six supernormal powers,
they dwell on the banks of the ocean; indeed, in their movement through the air, they are like those who travel by means of a ship.
And skilled in the marks,
seeking the supreme goal,
they then dwelt in the forest.
At that time, a perfectly enlightened Buddha named Sumedha appeared in the world,
out of compassion for us.
The Guide approached.
To the Great Hero who had arrived,
the Wise One, the Leader of the World;
Having prepared a grass mat,
I always gave it to the Supreme One in the World;
having gathered honey from the forest, I offered it.
Having always eaten together with the Best of Buddhas,
the Fully Enlightened One, after having partaken [of the meal],
spoke these words.
“I shall praise him who, with a confident heart and with his own hands, gave me that honey.”
Listen to me as I speak:
by this gift of honey and this bed of grass;
For thirty thousand eons he will delight in the world of the gods;
after those thirty thousand eons—
Born of the Okkāka clan,
he will be a teacher in the world named Gotama by lineage.
He is the heir to the Dhamma,
the legitimate son, fashioned by the Dhamma;
having fully understood all taints, he—
“...shall attain Nibbāna, free from taints.
Having come here from the world of the gods,
he has entered his mother’s womb.
It rained honey,
covering the earth with honey,
as soon as I had stepped forth.
And the womb is very difficult to cross;
even there, honey rains down for me,
raining at all times.
Having gone forth from the home,
I entered the homeless life;
I was a recipient of food and drink.
This is the fruit of giving honey:
having become one who has all desires fulfilled among gods and humans,
By that very gift of honey,
I have attained the destruction of the taints.
When the rain has fallen upon grass four inches deep,
When the trees are in full bloom and the ground is covered with them,
I dwell constantly, happy and free from taints, in empty houses, in pavilions, and at the foot of trees.
I have transcended all existence— both the middling and the great, as well as the inferior;
today my taints are exhausted.
Now there is no further becoming.
That gift which I gave back then, during thirty thousand eons—
I do not recognize an unhappy rebirth;
this is the fruit of giving honey.
The defilements have been burnt away by me.
All states of existence have been eradicated;
all taints are utterly exhausted;
now there is no further becoming.
Welcome indeed has come to me...
[and so on] ...the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
The four analytical knowledges... [and so forth]...
the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Thus indeed the venerable elder Madhudāyaka spoke these verses.
This is the fourth legend of the elder Madhudāyaka.
